findings.summary: New unconditional `SET TimeZone`/`SET DateStyle` statements can turn a previously working query into a BadRequestException
findings.evidence: `await client.query(`SET TimeZone = 'UTC'`)` and `await client.query(`SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'`)` are executed inside the same try block whose catch maps any error to `BadRequestException` (line 166-170). Any Postgres-wire-compatible target that rejects one of these GUCs (Redshift, older CockroachDB, pgbouncer in statement pooling mode, or a role with restricted SET) now fails *every* executeQuery call with 'Query execution failed', even though the user's SELECT itself is valid. Previously only `statement_timeout` was set. Wrapping these two session settings in their own try/catch (best-effort) would preserve the old behaviour.

findings.summary: RAW_TEXT_OIDS omits the array OIDs of the same date/time types, so array columns still yield JS Dates and a different string form
findings.evidence: RAW_TEXT_OIDS contains only DATE (1082), TIMESTAMP (1114) and TIMESTAMPTZ (1184). The array OIDs (_date 1182, _timestamp 1115, _timestamptz 1185) are not included, so `date[]`/`timestamp[]` columns are still run through pg's array parser, producing JS `Date` elements. Those flow into `toCell`, hit the `typeof val === 'object'` branch and are emitted as `["2025-06-15T00:00:00.000Z"]` — a different (and, for naive TIMESTAMP, timezone-shifted, since the array element parser interprets naive timestamps in the Node runtime TZ) representation than the scalar case the change was fixing.

findings.summary: Custom type parser ignores the `format` argument for the overridden OIDs, returning binary Buffers unparsed
findings.evidence: `datasourceTypeParser = (oid, format) => RAW_TEXT_OIDS.has(oid) ? (value: string) => value : getDefaultParser(oid, format)` — the identity parser is returned regardless of `format`. If pg ever requests results in binary format for these OIDs, the raw value is a Buffer, and the identity function returns the Buffer, which `toCell` then renders as `{"type":"Buffer","data":[...]}` instead of a date. The guard should be `format !== 'binary' && RAW_TEXT_OIDS.has(oid)`.

findings.summary: Leftover duplicate test: 'queries real tables with rows' now exists twice with contradictory expectations
findings.evidence: The diff adds a new `it('queries real tables with rows', ...)` at line 114 but the old copy at line 309 was not removed. Both create/TRUNCATE/DROP the same `_test_products` table in the shared DATABASE_URL database, and the stale copy still asserts the pre-change row shape (`{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: '9.99' }`). Jest silently runs both duplicate-named tests; the shared table makes them order-coupled (the first one DROPs the table the second recreates), so this is fragile as well as redundant — it looks like an incomplete replacement.

findings.summary: Connection leak: cleanup query inside `finally` is not itself guarded, so `rawClient.end()` can be skipped
findings.evidence: ```finally { await rawClient.query(`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ${table}`); await rawClient.end(); }``` — if the DROP rejects (connection already errored/terminated, e.g. after a statement_timeout or a failed CREATE leaving the session broken), the rejection propagates out of the `finally` and `rawClient.end()` never runs, leaking the pg connection and masking the original failure. The `end()` should be in its own `finally`/`catch`.

findings.summary: `toCell` can throw on values JSON.stringify rejects, aborting the whole result load
findings.evidence: `if (typeof val === 'object' && val !== null) return JSON.stringify(val);` — JSON.stringify throws TypeError on circular structures or values containing BigInt. `loadQueryResults` calls `toCell` per cell with no try/catch, so a single such value aborts the loop after `this.grid.clear()` (line 55) has already run, leaving the store empty and the query view broken rather than showing a degraded cell value.

findings.summary: Assertions weakened to `String(rows[0].n)` hold regardless of whether the type parser is correct
findings.evidence: The diff replaces `expect(queryResult.rows).toEqual([{ n: 1 }])` with `expect(String(rows[0].n)).toBe('1')` (and the same at the ownership test). `String()` yields '1' whether pg returns the number 1 or the string '1', so the assertion cannot fail if the new `types.getTypeParser` override accidentally starts stringifying INT4 — precisely the mechanism this PR introduces. The stricter original assertion still survives only in the older duplicate test at line 370.

findings.summary: Newly added test duplicates the name and body of an existing test ('queries real tables with rows') with weaker assertions
findings.evidence: The diff adds `it('queries real tables with rows', ...)` while the identical-named test already exists at packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:309, using the same `_test_products` table and the same inserts. The new copy asserts via `toCell(...)`/`String(...)` strings; the pre-existing one asserts exact typed rows. Two same-named tests creating/dropping the same table is confusing and adds no new coverage beyond the toCell mapping.

findings.summary: `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` is only covered by a mock-call assertion; no test would fail if the statement were dropped
findings.evidence: datasource.service.spec.ts:131 asserts only that client.query was called with the literal string — it re-asserts the implementation, not behavior. In the e2e type-map test the DATE/TIMESTAMP expectations ('2025-06-15', '2025-06-15 14:30:00') are the Postgres default DateStyle output, so removing the SET would leave every assertion green. (The TimeZone SET, by contrast, is genuinely observable via the TIMESTAMPTZ '+00' expectation.)

findings.summary: Unit test mocks away `createClient`, so the new `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` option and the RAW_TEXT_OIDS parser are never unit-tested

findings.evidence: packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:114 adds `it('queries real tables with rows', ...)` while the pre-existing test with the identical name survives at packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:309. Both create/TRUNCATE/DROP the shared `_test_products` table against the same DATABASE_URL database, and the new one DROPs it at the end while the old one re-CREATEs it — duplicated names make failures ambiguous and couple the two through shared DB state. findings.summary: Design doc's Query Execution / ReadOnlyStore sections still describe the pre-change value contract

findings.summary: User-visible rendering change for object-valued columns in the only production consumer of loadQueryResults
findings.evidence: packages/frontend/src/app/spreadsheet/datasource-view.tsx:108 calls `storeRef.current.loadQueryResults(res.columns, res.rows)`; with the new `toCell` (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:32-36) any object value now renders as JSON instead of `String(val)`. Over HTTP, pg arrays arrive as JS arrays (previously shown as `a,b`, now `["a","b"]`), JSON/JSONB columns previously `[object Object]` now show real JSON (an improvement), and bytea now renders `{"type":"Buffer","data":[...]}` — as the new e2e expectation at packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:236 documents. Also note the `val instanceof Date` branch is unreachable for this consumer, since values cross the HTTP/JSON boundary as strings; the only Date-producing path (pg) is exactly the one the backend change just stopped producing Dates on.

findings.summary: Duplicate test left behind: `it('queries real tables with rows')` now exists twice in the same describe block (new version at line 114, original at line 309). The original still asserts the pre-change result shape (`{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: '9.99' }`) while the new one asserts via `toCell`. The change clearly intended to replace the old test rather than add a near-verbatim copy (same table `_test_products`, same setup/cleanup, same name), so the suite now duplicates ~80 lines of DB fixture work and two identically-named tests coexist.

findings.summary: Partial/inconsistent fix for value fidelity: only DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ are pinned to raw Postgres text, while other pg types that the default parser turns into JS objects still flow through and end up JSON-stringified into sheet cells. The change's own e2e expectations enshrine this: BYTEA renders as `{"type":"Buffer","data":[222,173,190,239]}`, INTERVAL as `{"years":1,"months":2,"days":3}`, CIRCLE as `{"x":1,"y":2,"radius":3}`. If the intent is "cells show the value the database shows", these are user-visible wrong values left unaddressed; if the intent is only the timezone shift, the accepted JSON-blob rendering should be a stated decision (in the design doc) rather than an incidental test expectation.
findings.evidence: RAW_TEXT_OIDS contains only DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ; database.e2e-spec.ts type table asserts JSON-object cell values for BYTEA, INTERVAL, CIRCLE.

findings.summary: `toCell` is added to the public `@wafflebase/sheets` API surface but has no production consumer outside `readonly.ts`; the only external importer is a backend e2e test (`packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:8`). Widening a package's exported API purely to let a test re-derive expected values is a layering/taste concern — either keep it internal and assert on the store output, or if it is genuinely a shared query-value→cell conversion it belongs in the shared package (`@wafflebase/core`) rather than in `store/readonly.ts`. The name is also easy to confuse with the `Cell` type and the `toCellRect`/`toCellFont` family in `packages/sheets/src/view/*`, since it returns a `string`, not a `Cell`.
findings.evidence: packages/sheets/src/index.ts:197 exports `toCell`; only consumers are readonly.ts:73 and packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:175,301.

findings.summary: Scope: the new ~90-line exhaustive "all pg built-in types" table (with a commented-out inventory of internal/removed catalog OIDs) goes well beyond the date/time behavior this change fixes, and pins many expectations that are pg-driver rather than wafflebase behavior (MONEY locale formatting, BPCHAR padding, TSVECTOR normalization). It also DDLs (`CREATE`/`DROP TABLE _test_type_check`) inside the application's own DATABASE_URL database once per type. Worth trimming to the types this change actually alters.
findings.evidence: typeMap literal spanning roughly lines 214-275 with per-type DROP/CREATE/INSERT loop at 288-302.

findings.summary: SELECT-only validator is bypassable: it validates a comment-stripped COPY while executeQuery interpolates the ORIGINAL query text, enabling stacked-statement SQL injection (DROP/INSERT/etc.)
findings.evidence: validateSelectQuery (sql-validator.ts:28-31) strips `--...` comments into a separate string `withoutComments` and runs ALL checks (first-token, FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS, multi-statement) against that copy. datasource.service.ts:148 then builds `SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001` from the UNSTRIPPED `dto.query` and executes it at line 150 via `client.query(text)` with no parameter values, i.e. Postgres' simple query protocol, which permits multiple statements per message. Attack: an authenticated workspace member POSTs to /datasources/:id/query with query = SELECT 'x--', 1) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT (1 . The comment regex deletes from the `--` that sits INSIDE the string literal to end-of-line, so the validator only ever sees `SELECT 'x`: first token SELECT passes, no forbidden keyword remains (DROP was deleted), and the semicolon split yields one statement. The server then sends `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 'x--', 1) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT (1) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements — and the DROP runs with the datasource's stored credentials. The same trick smuggles INSERT/UPDATE/GRANT/COPY. Pre-existing code, but it is the guard protecting the exact executeQuery path this diff edits (lines 143-145).

findings.summary: TLS certificate validation disabled (`rejectUnauthorized: false`) when sslEnabled is set, so "SSL on" gives no MITM protection for datasource credentials or query results
findings.evidence: createClient sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (line 202, immediately above the `types:` option added by this diff at line 204). With rejectUnauthorized false the driver accepts any certificate, including a self-signed one presented by a network attacker, so an on-path attacker between the backend and the user's Postgres host can transparently intercept the connection, harvest the decrypted username/password sent at line 201 and read/modify all query results — while the UI still reports the connection as SSL-enabled. No CA/servername pinning option is exposed anywhere in CreateDataSourceDto (datasource.dto.ts:12-42).

findings.summary: SSRF: user-supplied host/port are connected to with no allowlist or private/link-local blocking, and connection errors are returned to the caller as a scan oracle
findings.evidence: CreateDataSourceDto only length-checks `host` (datasource.dto.ts:17-19) and range-checks `port` (1-65535); createClient (line 196-205) passes them straight to `new Client`. Any authenticated workspace member can create a datasource pointing at 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, or any internal RFC1918 host:port and call POST /datasources/:id/test; testConnection returns `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }` (line 121), which distinguishes ECONNREFUSED from timeout from protocol errors and thus enumerates internal services and open ports from inside the backend's network. `connectionTimeoutMillis: 10_000` (line 203) is the only limiter. Searched: grepped the datasource directory for localhost/127.0.0.1/169.254/allowlist/blocklist/private and read datasource.dto.ts, datasource.controller.ts and datasource.service.ts in full — no host validation exists on any path.

findings.summary: Raw Postgres driver error text is echoed back to API clients, disclosing internal hostnames, usernames, schema names and DB version details
findings.evidence: executeQuery catches any error and rethrows `new BadRequestException(pgError.message || 'Query execution failed')` (lines 166-170); testConnection likewise returns `error.message` verbatim (line 121). Postgres/driver messages routinely contain strings such as 'password authentication failed for user "x"', 'getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND internal-db.corp', or 'column "y" of relation "z" does not exist', handing an authenticated caller a schema/infrastructure enumeration primitive that also amplifies the SSRF oracle above.

findings.summary: New e2e tests run DDL (CREATE/TRUNCATE/DROP TABLE) against whatever database DATABASE_URL points at, risking destructive execution outside a throwaway test DB
findings.evidence: The added tests open a raw pg Client from `parseDatabaseUrl(process.env.DATABASE_URL!)` and issue `TRUNCATE _test_products RESTART IDENTITY`, `CREATE TABLE`, and repeated `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ${table}` (also in the all-types loop). Nothing asserts the target is an ephemeral/CI database, so anyone who runs the suite with a shared or production-adjacent DATABASE_URL destroys data in that database. Table names are constants, so this is not attacker-controlled — rated low confidence and minor, and it partly overlaps the test-quality lens.

verdict.reason: The quoted lines exist (datasource.service.ts:143-145, catch at :166-170), but the described failure mode is not reachable in this repository. (a) The product is PostgreSQL-only by explicit design — docs/design/sheets/datasource.md:25 lists non-PostgreSQL engines as a non-goal and :197 states "PostgreSQL only"; the model has no engine/dialect field (prisma/schema.prisma:15-30, port default 5432) and the driver is hard-wired to pg's Client (datasource.service.ts:6, :188-196). So the Redshift/older-CockroachDB cases are not supported targets. (b) On PostgreSQL, TimeZone and DateStyle are USERSET-context GUCs settable by any role in its own session, so the "role with restricted SET" case cannot fire, and `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` is the canonical documented form. (c) The one remaining scenario — a pooler that refuses SET entirely (pgbouncer statement pooling) — already fails one line earlier on the pre-existing `SET statement_timeout` at datasource.service.ts:143, which the finding itself concedes predates the change; therefore no previously-working executeQuery call is turned into a BadRequestException by lines 144-145. The premise "turns a previously working query into a BadRequestException" has no concrete instantiation. Counterexample to the claimed regression.

samples.summary: SELECT-only validator is bypassable: it validates a comment-stripped COPY while executeQuery interpolates the ORIGINAL query text, enabling stacked-statement SQL injection (DROP/INSERT/etc.)
samples.evidence: validateSelectQuery (sql-validator.ts:28-31) strips `--...` comments into a separate string `withoutComments` and runs ALL checks (first-token, FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS, multi-statement) against that copy. datasource.service.ts:148 then builds `SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001` from the UNSTRIPPED `dto.query` and executes it at line 150 via `client.query(text)` with no parameter values, i.e. Postgres' simple query protocol, which permits multiple statements per message. Attack: an authenticated workspace member POSTs to /datasources/:id/query with query = SELECT 'x--', 1) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT (1 . The comment regex deletes from the `--` that sits INSIDE the string literal to end-of-line, so the validator only ever sees `SELECT 'x`: first token SELECT passes, no forbidden keyword remains (DROP was deleted), and the semicolon split yields one statement. The server then sends `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 'x--', 1) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT (1) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements — and the DROP runs with the datasource's stored credentials. The same trick smuggles INSERT/UPDATE/GRANT/COPY. Pre-existing code, but it is the guard protecting the exact executeQuery path this diff edits (lines 143-145).

samples.summary: TLS certificate validation disabled (`rejectUnauthorized: false`) when sslEnabled is set, so "SSL on" gives no MITM protection for datasource credentials or query results

With rejectUnauthorized false the driver accepts any certificate, including a self-signed one presented by a network attacker, so an on-path attacker between the backend and the user's Postgres host can transparently intercept the connection, harvest the decrypted username/password sent at line 201 and read/modify all query results — while the UI still reports the connection as SSL-enabled.
